title: Lawrence v. Fox
summary: A creditor could enforce a promise made to his debtor for the creditor’s benefit even though the creditor supplied no consideration directly to the new promisor.
notes: The editors’ historical account questions the reported name “Holly” and explores the loan’s gambling background. The brief uses the parties and transaction as presented in the opinion; later historical findings are not silently made part of the adjudicated record.

sections.Parties: Holly owed money to Lawrence and became the promisee in the new arrangement. Fox borrowed money from Holly and promised to pay Lawrence. Lawrence was the intended recipient and plaintiff enforcing that promise.
sections.Material Facts: Holly advanced $300 to Fox and stated that he owed the same amount to Lawrence, payable the next day. In exchange for the loan, Fox promised Holly that he would pay Lawrence the next day. A bystander witnessed the transaction. Lawrence had not bargained directly with Fox and had furnished no consideration to Fox. The money Fox received became his own as a loan; it was not a segregated trust fund belonging to Lawrence.
sections.Procedural History: The trial court rejected Fox’s objections based on insufficient proof of the debt, lack of consideration, and lack of privity. A jury awarded Lawrence the loan amount and interest, and the intermediate court affirmed. The New York Court of Appeals affirmed by a six-to-two vote in 1859, although two of the six relied on agency rather than the broader beneficiary principle.
sections.Issue: Could Lawrence enforce Fox’s promise to Holly when Lawrence was neither the promisee nor the person who furnished consideration?
sections.Holding: The judgment for Lawrence was affirmed. The principal opinion recognized enforcement by a person for whose benefit a supported promise was made. The result did not require a trust fund or consideration supplied personally by the beneficiary.
sections.Reasoning:
The consideration question and the enforcement question were distinct. Holly’s loan supplied ample consideration for Fox’s promise. The remaining issue was whether Lawrence could enforce the resulting duty despite the absence of a direct bargain with Fox. The principal opinion relied on earlier New York authority allowing such enforcement and reasoned that the duty to pay the intended recipient was sufficiently established by the supported promise.

Trust cases supplied an analogy, but the principal opinion declined to make a trust asset essential. Fox’s ownership of the borrowed money did not eliminate the contractual duty to pay Lawrence. The possibility that Holly and Fox might have altered or released the obligation did not resolve this case because the relevant promise had not actually been released. Questions about when beneficiary rights become irrevocable remained for later development.

textbookImport.basis: Study paraphrase of the supplied tenth-edition casebook. No current-law/citator review.

learning.why: The three people perform different legal roles. Keeping those roles explicit explains how consideration can support a promise while someone other than its promisee enforces it.

topics.third-party-beneficiaries: Allows enforcement of a supported promise intended to discharge the promisee’s debt to a third person.
topics.consideration: The loan furnished by Holly supports the promise despite Lawrence’s lack of direct consideration.
topics.delegation: Holly arranges performance of the money obligation through Fox.
topics.assent: The supported agreement between promisor and promisee can create a right in a nonparty; beneficiary status is a separate question from bilateral assent.

learning.separateOpinions: Two concurring judges treated Holly as acting for Lawrence through an agency that Lawrence could ratify. The dissent insisted on privity or an interest in a trust asset and argued that Holly retained control over repayment. Thus the six judges agreeing on the result did not all adopt the same rationale.

mnemonic.rationale: Three hundred dollars lent for a day
